---
title: "The 6-Layer Architecture"
subtitle: "Progressive Lowering: From Abstract Demand to Concrete Supply"
---

MLSys·im organizes the full ML systems domain into six composable layers. Abstract workload *demand* (Layer A) is progressively mapped onto concrete hardware, infrastructure, distributed systems, and cyber-physical platforms (Layers B--D and F) through analytical *solvers* (Layer E). Each layer corresponds directly to chapters in the [Machine Learning Systems](https://mlsysbook.ai) textbook and its companion [lecture slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/).

Understanding this stack is the foundation for working with both this library and the textbook it accompanies.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Values on this page come from the MLSys·im registries, so they cannot drift.
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Hardware, Infrastructure, Models

grids = Infrastructure.Grids
ci_quebec = grids.Quebec.carbon_intensity_g_kwh
ci_poland = grids.Poland.carbon_intensity_g_kwh
ci_us = grids.US_Avg.carbon_intensity_g_kwh
ci_spread = ci_poland / ci_quebec
_n_hw = len(Hardware.list())
```

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%%
%%| fig-cap: "The MLSys·im 6-Layer Stack. Workloads (demand) are lowered onto Hardware, Infrastructure, Systems, and Embodied platforms (supply). Solvers bridge demand and supply to produce typed analytical profiles."
%%| fig-width: 100%
flowchart TB
    A["<b>Layer A · Workloads</b> — <i>Demand</i><br/>Transformer · SparseTransformer · CNN · SSM · Diffusion · Embodied<br/>Parameters · FLOPs · Arithmetic Intensity"]
    B["<b>Layer B · Hardware</b> — <i>Silicon</i><br/>HardwareNode · ComputeCore · MemoryHierarchy<br/>Peak FLOP/s · Bandwidth · Capacity · TDP"]
    C["<b>Layer C · Infrastructure</b> — <i>Environment</i><br/>GridProfile · Datacenter<br/>Carbon Intensity · PUE · WUE"]
    D["<b>Layer D · Systems</b> — <i>Topology</i><br/>Node · Fleet · NetworkFabric<br/>Topology · Accelerators/Node · Fabric BW"]
    F_emb["<b>Layer F · Embodied &amp; Physical AI</b> — <i>Cyber-Physical</i><br/>Embodied · Sensors · Actuators · Agents<br/>Stopping Envelopes · Control Loops · Safety Leases"]
    E["<b>Layer E · Solvers</b> — <i>Analysis</i><br/>SingleNode · Distributed · Serving<br/>Economics · Sustainability · Robotics · Agents"]
    R["<b>Results</b><br/>PerformanceProfile · AnalyticalResult (*Result)"]

    A --> E
    B --> D
    C --> D
    D --> E
    F_emb --> E
    E --> R

    style E fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,stroke-width:2px
```

The flow reads top-to-bottom: a **Workload** (the computation to perform) and a **System** (the available hardware, network, and environment) feed into a **Solver** (the analytical engine), which returns quantitative results that can guide a design decision.

::: {.callout-note}
## Physics formulas
Closed-form equations live in **`mlsysim.physics.*`** (performance, memory, communication,
serving, economics, reliability, robotics, and fundamental physical constants in
`mlsysim.physics.constants`). Pint units live in **`mlsysim.core.units`**; chip, model,
scenario, and system specs live only in their registries (the legacy `core/constants.py`
catch-all module was retired). See [Math Foundations](math.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Two views of the same package
The six layers are the *runtime* view: how demand meets supply through solvers.
The registries that populate Layers A--D and Layer F are organized as **twelve zoos**
(Hardware, Models, Datasets, Platforms, Infrastructure, Systems, Ops, Scenarios, Embodied, Sensors, Actuators, Agents)
plus support namespaces. That *data* view is documented in
[DATA_MODEL.md](DATA_MODEL.md). Both descriptions are true at different altitudes.
:::

## Layer A: Workloads (Demand) {#sec-layer-a}

A **Workload** is a hardware-agnostic description of computational demand. It states how many FLOPs and memory bytes Llama-3 *requires*, not how fast Llama-3 runs.

MLSys·im provides six concrete workload types (plus the base `Workload` class):

- **`TransformerWorkload`**: Dense LLMs and attention-based models (GPT, Llama, BERT). Defined by parameter count, layer count, hidden dimension, attention/KV heads, and sequence length. Supports KV-cache size estimation for autoregressive inference.
- **`SparseTransformerWorkload`**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformers (Mixtral, DeepSeek) with total vs. active parameter accounting and expert-routing metadata.
- **`CNNWorkload`**: Vision and convolutional models (ResNet, MobileNet, YOLO). Defined by parameter count and total FLOPs per forward pass.
- **`SSMWorkload`**: State-space sequence models (Mamba) with recurrent state sizing independent of context length.
- **`DiffusionWorkload`**: Multi-step iterative denoising architectures (Stable Diffusion, DiT).
- **`EmbodiedWorkload`**: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and sensorimotor policies operating under closed-loop control deadlines.

The key step comes when a workload is "lowered" at a specific numerical precision (FP32, FP16, INT8, INT4). This precision lowering determines the **Arithmetic Intensity** (FLOPs/Byte), the single ratio that decides whether a model will be compute-bound or memory-bound on any given hardware target.

::: {.callout-note}

## Layer B: Hardware (Silicon) {#sec-layer-b}

A **`HardwareNode`** represents a single physical accelerator, such as an H100 GPU, an Apple M3 chip, a Jetson Orin, or even an ESP32 microcontroller. It provides the raw physical supply:

- **Compute:** Peak throughput (TFLOP/s) across precisions (FP32, FP16, INT8), modeled via `ComputeCore`.
- **Memory:** HBM or SRAM capacity and transfer bandwidth (TB/s), modeled via `MemoryHierarchy`.
- **Power:** Thermal Design Power (TDP) in watts.

Every piece of silicon has a **ridge point**, the ratio of peak compute to memory bandwidth ($I^* = \text{Peak\_FLOPs} / \text{BW}$). When a workload's arithmetic intensity falls below this ridge point, the workload is memory-bound: the compute units starve waiting for data. When above, the workload is compute-bound: memory delivers data faster than the cores can consume it.

This is the Roofline model, the diagnostic framework at the heart of Layer E's `SingleNodeModel`.

::: {.callout-note}

## Layer C: Infrastructure (Environment) {#sec-layer-c}

Hardware does not run in a vacuum. It runs in datacenters plugged into regional power grids, cooled by air or liquid systems, and constrained by physical energy budgets.

A **`GridProfile`** captures this physical context:

- **Carbon intensity** (g CO₂/kWh) varies about `{python} f"{ci_spread:.0f}"`× across regions. Quebec's hydroelectric grid produces about `{python} f"{ci_quebec:.0f}"` g CO₂/kWh; Poland's coal-dominated grid produces about `{python} f"{ci_poland:.0f}"` g CO₂/kWh.
- **Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE)** is the ratio of total facility power to IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.1 means 10% overhead for cooling and infrastructure; 1.6 means 60%.
- **Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE)** is the liters of on-site cooling water consumed per kWh of IT equipment energy ($E_{\text{IT}} \times \text{WUE}_{\text{site}}$), determined by cooling technology (closed-loop air/liquid vs. evaporative towers).

A 1000-watt GPU running identical computations in Quebec versus Poland produces vastly different carbon footprints. This layer makes that difference quantifiable.

::: {.callout-note}

## Layer D: Systems (Topology) {#sec-layer-d}

A single GPU cannot train a 100-billion-parameter model. Layer D composes individual `HardwareNode`s from Layer B into distributed clusters, connected by the network fabrics that determine communication overhead.

Core system types include:

- **`Node`**: A single compute server grouping accelerators within a physical chassis (e.g., 8x H100 GPUs connected by 450 GB/s per-direction / 900 GB/s bidirectional NVLink). Includes one-way `intra_node_bw` and NIC count.
- **`RackProfile`**: A physical rack composition that aggregates node count, accelerator count, accelerator power, and non-accelerator support power.
- **`NetworkFabric`**: The inter-node interconnect: topology (fat-tree, rail-optimized), bandwidth (e.g., 400 Gbps InfiniBand NDR), latency, and oversubscription ratio.
- **`Fleet`**: A collection of `Node`s connected by a `NetworkFabric`, deployed in a specific `Datacenter` (Layer C). This is the complete system that solvers operate on.

The structure of this system (how many GPUs each node holds, what fabric connects them, and which parallelism strategy runs across them) determines its communication overhead and scaling efficiency.

::: {.callout-note}

## Layer E: Solvers (Analysis) {#sec-layer-e}

The previous four layers are static definitions, the nouns of the stack. **Solvers** are its verbs: the analytical engines that bridge demand and supply to answer specific questions.

Each solver implements closed-form equations from peer-reviewed systems literature. They require no simulation, no benchmarking, and no hardware.

| Solver | Bridges | Core Equation | Key Output |
|:-------|:--------|:--------------|:-----------|
| **SingleNodeModel** | A $\to$ B | Roofline / Iron Law (Williams et al., 2009) | Latency, throughput, bottleneck classification |
| **DistributedModel** | A $\to$ D | Ring All-Reduce + Pipeline schedules | Scaling efficiency, communication overhead, bubble fraction |
| **ServingModel** | A $\to$ B | Pre-fill / Decode phase decomposition | TTFT, inter-token latency, KV-cache memory |
| **EconomicsModel** | D $\to$ cost | CapEx + OpEx over time horizon | TCO in USD, cost per query |
| **SustainabilityModel** | D $\to$ C | PUE $\times$ grid carbon intensity | Energy (kWh), carbon (kg CO₂e), water (L) |
| **ReliabilityModel** | D $\to$ uptime | Young-Daly optimal checkpointing | Fleet MTBF, failure probability, checkpoint interval |

Solvers are composable. To find the most sustainable way to serve Llama-70B, chain `ServingModel` (feasibility and latency) into `EconomicsModel` (cost) into `SustainabilityModel` (carbon). Each solver's typed output feeds naturally into the next.

::: {.callout-note}

## Layer F: Embodied & Physical AI {#sec-layer-f}

Physical and agentic AI systems couple neural inference to real-time control loops, sensors, actuators, and tool-use environments:

- **`Embodied`, `Sensors`, and `Actuators`**: Quadrupeds, humanoids, manipulators, drones, AMRs, autonomous vehicles, cameras, LiDARs, IMUs, safety scanners/light curtains, harmonic drives, quasi-direct drives, and safety relays.
- **`Agents`**: Multi-step tool-calling, deliberation, coding, research, and remediation harnesses with context-window and verification economics.
- **`mlsysim.physics.robotics` & `mlsysim.solvers`**: Closed-form stopping-distance envelopes, kinematic limits, sensor-fusion timing budgets, thermal/battery endurance, and safety assurance bounds.

::: {.callout-note .mls-unreleased}
## Textbook, labs, and slides (Volumes III & IV Preview)

## Progressive Lowering in Action

The architecture is best understood through a concrete example. Consider the question: **"Can I serve INT4 Llama-3-70B replicas across a 4-H100 node within a target annual budget while minimizing carbon?"**

This single question touches Layers A--E (with Layer F extending the same pattern when an inference loop drives an agent harness or robot controller):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
llama = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
print(f"""```text
1. Layer A — Llama-3-70B workload: {llama.parameters.magnitude / 1e9:.1f}B parameters, GQA with {llama.kv_heads} KV heads,
             ~{llama.size_in_bytes("fp16").to("GB").magnitude:.0f} GB at FP16 (~{llama.size_in_bytes("int4").to("GB").magnitude:.0f} GB raw INT4)

2. Layer B — H100 hardware: {h100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude:.0f} TFLOP/s (FP16), {h100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude:.2f} TB/s HBM3,
             {h100.memory.capacity.to("GiB").magnitude:.0f} GiB capacity, {h100.tdp.to("W").magnitude:.0f} W TDP

3. Layer C — Infrastructure: choose between Quebec ({ci_quebec:.0f} g CO₂/kWh)
             and US Average ({ci_us:.0f} g CO₂/kWh)

4. Layer D — System: 1 node × 4 H100s (or sharded TP across NVLink {h100.nvlink.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude:.0f} GB/s via DistributedModel)

5. Layer E — Chain solvers:
             ServingModel / ServingCapacityModel → single-GPU TTFT, ITL, KV feasibility & replica count
             EconomicsModel → TCO over 1 year
             SustainabilityModel → carbon & water footprint by region
```""")
```

Each layer contributes a different piece of the answer. No single layer is sufficient alone. This is why MLSys·im separates concerns into six composable layers rather than offering a monolithic "predict performance" function.
